parts.name: Anterior horn
parts.function_note: the meniscal attachment most variable in size/shape between the medial and lateral menisci.
parts.source: Fox AJ, Bedi A, Rodeo SA (2012) 'The basic science of human knee menisci: structure, composition, and function.' Sports Health 4(4):340-351 -- meniscal horn/body anatomy, vascularity zones, and load-transmission role.

parts.name: Body
parts.attachment_or_location: peripheral rim, attached to the joint capsule (and, for the medial meniscus, the deep MCL)
parts.function_note: the load-bearing central segment; only the outer ~10-30% is vascularized (the 'red-red' zone), the inner majority is avascular and has limited independent healing capacity after tearing.
parts.source: Fox AJ, Bedi A, Rodeo SA (2012) 'The basic science of human knee menisci: structure, composition, and function.' Sports Health 4(4):340-351 -- meniscal horn/body anatomy, vascularity zones, and load-transmission role.

parts.name: Posterior horn
parts.function_note: the region of the medial meniscus's posterior horn is a common site of degenerative tears, particularly with age.
parts.source: Fox AJ, Bedi A, Rodeo SA (2012) 'The basic science of human knee menisci: structure, composition, and function.' Sports Health 4(4):340-351 -- meniscal horn/body anatomy, vascularity zones, and load-transmission role.

function: A C-shaped (medial) or more circular (lateral) fibrocartilaginous wedge deepening the tibial plateau, less mobile than the lateral meniscus due to its firm capsular and deep MCL attachments -- a structural reason it is torn substantially more often than the lateral meniscus.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Fox AJ, Bedi A, Rodeo SA (2012) 'The basic science of human knee menisci: structure, composition, and function.' Sports Health 4(4):340-351 -- meniscal horn/body anatomy, vascularity zones, and load-transmission role.

function: A C-shaped (medial) or more circular (lateral) fibrocartilaginous wedge deepening the tibial plateau, more mobile than the medial meniscus (no firm collateral-ligament attachment, and interrupted posteriorly by the popliteus tendon hiatus), which correlates with its lower injury frequency.
